heuristics.condition: When a Canadian spouse seeks divorce on the ground of separation
heuristics.action: The application may be filed before 12 months elapse, but the divorce cannot be granted until a full 12 months of separation has passed
heuristics.because: The Divorce Act requires that spouses have separated and lived apart for at least one year before a separation-based divorce can be finalized
heuristics.regulatory_basis: Department of Justice Canada — Divorce Act fact sheet, separation period requirement

heuristics.rule: At least one spouse must have resided in a Canadian province or territory for at least one year before applying
heuristics.condition: When either spouse files for divorce under the federal Divorce Act
heuristics.action: Confirm that at least one spouse meets the one-year provincial/territorial residency requirement before filing
heuristics.because: If neither spouse meets the residency requirement, divorce under the federal Divorce Act is unavailable
heuristics.regulatory_basis: Department of Justice Canada — Divorce Act fact sheet, residency requirement

heuristics.rule: No-fault separation ground is the dominant path; fault-based grounds (cruelty, adultery) require proof and are rarely pursued
heuristics.condition: When a Canadian spouse is choosing which ground to cite for divorce
heuristics.action: Default to the separation ground unless there is a specific legal reason to pursue cruelty or adultery, as those require evidentiary proof
heuristics.because: The existence of the one-year no-fault separation path makes fault-based grounds procedurally burdensome without commensurate benefit in the vast majority of cases
heuristics.regulatory_basis: Department of Justice Canada — Divorce Act fact sheet, three grounds for divorce

heuristics.rule: Use 'parenting arrangements' terminology, not 'custody and access', for post-divorce child arrangements
heuristics.condition: When describing where children will live and how decisions about them are made in any Canadian divorce proceeding on or after March 1, 2021
heuristics.action: Apply the term 'parenting arrangements' as defined under the amended Divorce Act
heuristics.because: The Divorce Act was amended effective March 1, 2021 to replace 'custody and access' with 'parenting arrangements', reflecting a statutory reframing of child-related decisions
heuristics.regulatory_basis: Department of Justice Canada — Divorce Act fact sheet, terminology shift effective March 1, 2021

decision_factors.why_it_matters: The chosen ground determines the evidentiary burden and the timeline to finalization — separation requires waiting one year but no proof of fault; cruelty and adultery require proof but have no mandatory waiting period stated
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Identify whether the filing spouse can establish one year of separation (no fault required) versus whether they have provable evidence of cruelty or adultery

decision_factors.factor: One-year provincial/territorial residency of at least one spouse
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Residency of at least one spouse for at least one year in a Canadian province or territory is a threshold eligibility requirement — without it, the federal Divorce Act does not apply
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Confirm the physical residence history of both spouses; if neither has resided in Canada for one year, the Divorce Act route is unavailable

decision_factors.why_it_matters: The 12-month clock for separation-based divorce runs from the date of separation — establishing this date precisely determines when finalization is legally possible
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Identify the date on which spouses separated and began living apart; the divorce cannot be finalized until 12 months after that date

decision_factors.factor: Presence of children and parenting arrangements
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Canadian divorce proceedings must address where children will live and how decisions about them will be made under the 'parenting arrangements' framework introduced March 1, 2021
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Determine whether the couple has dependent children and whether parenting arrangements have been or can be agreed upon or adjudicated

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Leaving a Canadian marriage and pursuing divorce
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The minimum legal runway to a finalized divorce is at least 12 months from separation — a person who decides to leave cannot legally finalize a divorce in less than one year under the separation ground, which is the predominant route; this timeline is structurally longer than some US state equivalents
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Any spouse in a Canadian marriage who believes that separating means a quick legal resolution; particularly affects those who want to remarry or need a finalized divorce for immigration, financial, or personal reasons

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Filing for divorce before the 12 months of separation elapse
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Filing early is permitted, but the divorce cannot be granted until the full 12-month separation period is complete — early filing does not accelerate the finalization date
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Spouses who assume that filing promptly will shorten the overall timeline

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Pursuing a fault-based ground (cruelty or adultery) to avoid the one-year wait
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Fault-based grounds require proof, introducing evidentiary burden and litigation complexity that the separation route avoids entirely — the time and cost of proving fault may exceed the time saved by bypassing the one-year period
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Spouses who believe citing cruelty or adultery will result in a faster or more advantageous divorce outcome

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Relocating outside Canada before filing for divorce
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: If neither spouse has resided in a Canadian province or territory for at least one year, divorce under the federal Divorce Act becomes unavailable — only limited alternatives under the Civil Marriage Act may apply in specific cases
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Spouses who have emigrated or are considering emigrating before resolving their marital status legally

failure_patterns.pattern: Attempting to finalize a separation-based divorce before 12 months of living apart have elapsed
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The Divorce Act mandates that the full one-year separation period must have passed before a divorce on the separation ground can be granted — courts cannot grant the divorce earlier regardless of when the application was filed
failure_patterns.consequence: Divorce cannot be granted; the application cannot proceed to finalization until the 12-month period is complete
warning_signs: Separation date is less than 12 months before the anticipated finalization hearing
Parties assume filing date starts the clock rather than the separation date

failure_patterns.pattern: Filing for divorce under the Divorce Act when neither spouse meets the one-year Canadian residency requirement
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The Act requires at least one spouse to have resided in a Canadian province or territory for at least one year — without this, the court lacks jurisdiction under the Act
failure_patterns.consequence: Divorce under the federal Divorce Act is unavailable; only limited alternatives under the Civil Marriage Act may exist for specific cases
warning_signs: Both spouses have recently immigrated or emigrated
Neither spouse has maintained a one-year residence in any Canadian province or territory

diagnostic_questions.question: Has at least one spouse resided in a Canadian province or territory for at least one year?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the threshold residency requirement under the Divorce Act is satisfied — without this, the Act does not apply
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Proceed to assess which ground for divorce applies and whether the separation period has been met
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Divorce under the federal Divorce Act is unavailable; explore whether limited alternatives under the Civil Marriage Act apply

diagnostic_questions.question: Have the spouses been separated and living apart for at least 12 months?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the separation-based ground — the predominant no-fault path — is available for finalization
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: The separation ground is available; the divorce application can be finalized
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: The divorce cannot yet be finalized on separation grounds; determine exact separation date to calculate when finalization becomes possible, or assess whether a fault-based ground with evidentiary proof is being pursued

diagnostic_questions.question: Is the divorce being sought on the ground of cruelty or adultery rather than separation?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the filing spouse is prepared to meet an evidentiary burden of proof, as both fault-based grounds require proof
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Assess whether sufficient evidence exists to establish cruelty or adultery to the court's standard; note that these grounds are rarely pursued given the availability of the no-fault separation route
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Confirm the separation date and proceed under the one-year separation ground

diagnostic_questions.question: Are there dependent children whose living arrangements and decision-making must be addressed?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether parenting arrangements — the statutory term under the Divorce Act as of March 1, 2021 — must be established as part of the divorce proceeding
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Parenting arrangements must be addressed; use the terminology and framework in force since March 1, 2021, not the former 'custody and access' language
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Child-related arrangements are not required; proceed with the divorce on the applicable ground

diagnostic_questions.question: Has the divorce application been filed before the 12-month separation period is complete?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the applicant understands that early filing is permitted but does not accelerate the finalization date
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Confirm that the applicant understands finalization cannot occur until the full 12 months have elapsed from the date of separation
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: No issue — filing after 12 months means finalization can proceed without a waiting period post-filing

industry_realities.common_belief: You must wait until after the full 12-month separation period before you can file for divorce in Canada
industry_realities.actual_reality: The Divorce Act permits filing before the 12-month separation period is complete — the restriction is on finalization, not on filing
industry_realities.implication: A spouse can initiate the legal process early while the separation period runs, potentially reducing overall time to finalization after the 12 months elapse

industry_realities.common_belief: Proving adultery or cruelty in a Canadian divorce gives the accusing spouse legal or financial advantages over using the separation ground
industry_realities.actual_reality: The source identifies cruelty and adultery as rarely pursued precisely because the no-fault separation route exists and fault-based grounds require proof — no advantage from fault grounds is stated
industry_realities.implication: In the absence of a specific strategic reason, the separation ground is the standard path; pursuing fault grounds introduces evidentiary complexity without a stated benefit

industry_realities.common_belief: Post-divorce child arrangements in Canada are still governed by 'custody and access' terminology
industry_realities.actual_reality: Effective March 1, 2021, the Divorce Act replaced 'custody and access' with 'parenting arrangements' — the old terminology is no longer the operative legal framework
industry_realities.implication: Any divorce proceedings, agreements, or legal documents referencing child arrangements must use 'parenting arrangements' language to conform to the current Act

industry_realities.common_belief: Either spouse can file for divorce in Canada regardless of where they currently live
industry_realities.actual_reality: At least one spouse must have resided in a Canadian province or territory for at least one year; if neither spouse meets this requirement, the federal Divorce Act is unavailable
industry_realities.implication: Spouses who have both relocated outside Canada must verify residency eligibility before assuming the Divorce Act applies to their situation

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Assumes that the 12-month clock starts when the divorce application is filed, or that filing immediately triggers eligibility for finalization
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Knows that the 12-month clock runs from the date of separation (living apart), that filing can occur before 12 months elapse, but that finalization is legally blocked until the full period passes
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Misjudging the timeline leads to incorrect expectations about when a divorce can be legally completed, affecting financial, immigration, and personal planning

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Considers citing adultery or cruelty to avoid the one-year wait or to gain advantage, without accounting for the evidentiary burden those grounds impose
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Recognizes that fault-based grounds require proof and are rarely pursued in practice because the no-fault separation route exists; defaults to separation unless there is a specific, evidence-backed reason to use a fault ground
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Pursuing a fault ground without sufficient evidence introduces procedural complexity and potential failure without a commensurate benefit

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Assumes that being married in Canada or having a Canadian marriage certificate is sufficient to file for divorce under the Divorce Act regardless of current residence
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Verifies that at least one spouse has resided in a Canadian province or territory for at least one year before filing, and knows that the Act is unavailable if neither spouse meets this threshold
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Filing without meeting the residency requirement means the court lacks jurisdiction under the Act, and the application cannot proceed

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Uses 'custody and access' language in legal documents and proceedings because it was the longstanding standard terminology
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Applies 'parenting arrangements' as the operative statutory term effective March 1, 2021, and ensures all documents and agreements reflect the current Act language
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Using superseded terminology may create ambiguity or non-conformance with the current legal framework in Canadian divorce proceedings
